systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.
Source : The Ritz Herald
Rubrique : Sanctions et export
Date du flux : 07/11/2026
Auteur : Helen Roscha
Titre d'origine : Treasury Sanctions Eight Canadian Money Services Businesses Enabling Iranian Regime Sanctions Evasion

ARTICLE :
SOURCE 1 (The Ritz Herald) :
The Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control on November 6 designated eight money services businesses based in Canada that enable the Iranian regime, sanctioned entities associated with the regime, and other illicit actors that move assets into and out of Iran.
As part of Operation Economic Outcast, the action targets companies that facilitate the exchange of Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets to enable international transactions involving Iran. Many of these businesses have facilitated transactions with sanctioned Iranian digital asset exchanges, as well as with digital asset addresses associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The State Department described the designations as action against eight digital asset service providers that help the Iranian regime evade sanctions and fund terrorism.
“Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “Treasury will pursue and disrupt the Iranian regime’s financial channels anywhere in the world.”
The designated entities are Diverse Trade Inc (doing business as Million Exchange), 1380079 BC Limited and Top PC Technician Inc (both doing business as Amin Exchange), NIA Nations Currency Ltd, 2397639 Ontario Ltd (doing business as Farah Exchange), CCC Inc, B Galaxy Inc (doing business as Cryptoyal), and Darvish Exchange. Several of the targets also worked with narco-trafficker and former Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, who was apprehended in January 2026. Wedding used money exchange businesses in the Vancouver and Toronto areas to launder billions of dollars in drug proceeds, converting cash to digital assets for transfer abroad.
This action was coordinated with the Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and FINTRAC, Canada’s financial intelligence unit, as well as the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). It reflects the Trump Administration’s whole-of-government effort to combat the illicit use of digital assets for drug trafficking. The designations follow previous OFAC sanctions on Iranian digital asset exchanges, including the June 2, 2026 designations of Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin, and Ramzinex, and the August 7, 2026 designations of Aban Tether Exchange and SHPS Shelbit.
The State Department noted that several of the designated businesses also laundered proceeds from drug trafficking, showing how the same illicit networks serve both Iran and criminal organizations. As part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched in August to sever economic lifelines sustaining the Iranian regime and its IRGC, the United States will continue to cut off revenue used for terrorism, weapons proliferation, and proxies. The designations are imposed pursuant to Executive Order 13902, which targets the Iranian digital asset sector among other key sectors of the Iranian economy.
As a result of this action, all property and interests in property of the designated persons that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked. OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S. persons or within the United States that involve any property or interests in property of designated persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in civil or criminal penalties.

SOURCE 2 (ASHARQ AL-AWSAT English) :
The United States on Friday announced a new round of sanctions targeting networks and entities connected to Iran, according to a notification published on the US Department of the Treasury’s website.
“Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated eight money services businesses based in Canada that enable the Iranian regime, sanctioned entities associated with the regime, and other illicit actors that move assets into and out of Iran,” it wrote.
The sanctions effectively cut the firms off from the dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets that the firms may have in the United States and prohibiting any transactions with US persons or entities.
The actions are the latest in a series of Treasury moves against firms outside the United States that it says help Iran get around US sanctions, as Washington keeps up pressure on Tehran.
“Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “Treasury will pursue and disrupt the Iranian regime’s financial channels anywhere in the world.”
The Treasury identified the designated businesses in Ontario and British Columbia as Diverse Trade Inc doing business as Million Exchange, 1380079 BC Limited, Top PC Technician Inc, NIA Nations Currency Ltd, 2397639 Ontario Ltd doing business as Farah Exchange, CCC Inc and B Galaxy Inc and Darvish Exchange.
Separately, the Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network division issued an order that also cuts off virtual currency exchanger MEXC Global from the US financial system over transactions that it says are linked to sanctions evasion by Iran, North Korea and Russia.
FinCEN, the Treasury's anti-money laundering unit, said that the order prevents US financial institutions from processing fund transfers involving Seychelles-incorporated MEXC Global, which it says has facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions linked to Iran, North Korea and Russia as well as transactions with other sanctioned actors.

SOURCE 3 (Anadolu Ajansı) :
US sanctions 8 Canadian money services businesses for alleged role in Iranian sanctions evasion
Treasury Department says several targets also worked with narcotrafficker, former Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding
Merve Aydogan
07 November 2026•Update: 07 November 2026
HAMILTON, Canada
The US Treasury Department sanctioned eight Canada-based money services businesses on Friday that it accused of enabling the Iranian government and moving assets into and out of Iran.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) said the action is part of Operation Economic Outcast and was imposed under Executive Order 13902, which targets the Iranian digital asset sector.
The firms allegedly exchange Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets, and many are accused of dealing with sanctioned Iranian exchanges and addresses linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. "Treasury will pursue and disrupt the Iranian regime’s financial channels anywhere in the world."
The designated entities are Diverse Trade Inc, doing business as Million Exchange; 1380079 BC Limited, doing business as Amin Exchange; Top PC Technician Inc; NIA Nations Currency Ltd; 2397639 Ontario Ltd, doing business as Farah Exchange; CCC Inc; B Galaxy Inc, doing business as Cryptoyal; and Darvish Exchange.
The Treasury Department said Million Exchange addresses allegedly sent the equivalent of hundreds of thousands of dollars to IRGC-linked or terrorism-related addresses. Addresses tied to Farah Exchange allegedly sent millions of dollars in digital assets to addresses associated with Ryan Wedding.
It said Wedding, a sanctioned Canadian drug trafficker apprehended in January, used money exchange businesses in the Vancouver and Toronto areas to launder billions of dollars in drug proceeds. Amin Exchange allegedly laundered drug proceeds for him in Vancouver, converting cash into digital assets he directed abroad.
The action follows OFAC designations of Iranian exchanges Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin and Ramzinex on June 2, and Aban Tether Exchange and SHPS Shelbit on Aug. 7. It was coordinated with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Canada’s financial intelligence unit FINTRAC and the Drug Enforcement Administration.
In a separate statement, the State Department said the US took action against "eight digital asset service providers that help the Iranian regime evade sanctions and fund terrorism." It said some firms changed names and addresses to avoid detection, and that "Anyone, anywhere in the world, who helps Tehran evade sanctions risks being held accountable."
The Treasury Department said the businesses remained operational despite media reports highlighting sanctions-evasion and terrorist-financing risks.
